knowledge: I heard the doctor say I'm depressed, even though I kept saying I'm not, and it felt like no one was listening to me.
I was there in the living room with my mom and the doctor, sitting through another appointment where they talked about my condition while I just wanted to go back to my book.
I narrated that my depression isn't a side effect of cancer—it's a side effect of dying.
I kept telling myself and everyone else that I'm not depressed, because I know my feelings come from the reality of dying, not from the cancer itself.
I looked up from my book when I heard a laugh, saw a guy spinning a girl around playfully, and then I went back to reading.
I sat on the exam table, my legs dangling, repeating 'I'm not depressed' while Mom listed off everything I did wrong and the doctor ignored me, like my words didn't even matter.

knowledge: The doctor told me he might switch me to Zoloft or Lexapro and have me take it twice a day instead of once.
When the doctor suggested increasing my medication, I shot back with 'Why stop there?' and said I could take it—I'm like the Keith Richards of cancer kids.
I was there with my mom and the doctor, talking about my mental health and treatment options, and later he asked if I’d been going to that support group.
I challenged the doctor when he called my illness a 'journey'—I said, 'Journey? Really?'—because that word felt fake and overused, like it was supposed to make everything sound meaningful.
I remember the doctor asking me again about going to that support group he suggested, and I told him I wasn't sure it was for me, but he kept pushing, saying it would help me connect with others.
I remember the doctor dismissing what I said and insisting I try the support group, ending with 'For me'—so I felt I had to agree, even though I didn't want to.

I said I wasn't depressed, but the doctor just talked over me, calling it a 'journey' like it was some kind of adventure—Mom and he had already decided for me, and I could tell there was no point fighting it.

I told the group, 'I'm, uh, Hazel. 16. Thyroid originally but with quite the impressive satellite colony in my lungs,' and my voice sounded distant to me.
After I shared, I heard everyone say together, 'We're here for you,' and I remember thinking how strange it was that they said it like they meant it.

My parents insisted I needed to get out of the house and be a teenager, so they made me go to support group despite my objections.
I told my parents that if they really wanted me to be a teenager, they should buy me a fake ID so I could go to clubs and drink gimlets instead of going to support group.

I said, 'You can't make me,' even though I knew they would win — it was just another stupid support group they thought would fix me.

knowledge: I sat in the Circle of Sick, surrounded by others who, like me, were just trying to get through another day.
I heard Isaac say he was facing another surgery soon and that it would likely leave him blind, and I remember how he tried to downplay it, but I could feel how much it weighed on him.
I felt the Beautiful Boy's gaze on me while Isaac was talking, and it was hard to focus, so I decided to meet his stare head-on.
I think I won the staring contest with him because I held my gaze just as firmly, even though I can't be totally sure he gave up first.
I remember Augustus introducing himself, saying he was 17 and had lost a leg to osteosarcoma a year and a half ago, but was now in remission.
I heard Augustus say he wants to live an extraordinary life and be remembered, and that his greatest fear is not doing that — it's oblivion.
I told Augustus that oblivion is inevitable for everyone, even people like Cleopatra or Mozart, and that fearing it doesn't make sense because eventually no one will remember any of us anyway.

I locked eyes with that boy—Augustus—and refused to look away, even though his stare made my skin prickle. I won that stupid silent contest without blinking, and for a second, I felt something sharp and real cut through the numbness.

I don’t remember exactly when I raised my hand, but Patrick’s surprise told me it was out of character. The words about oblivion just came out—cold and clear—and for once, I didn’t care if it scared people.
